idiom_name: nil (NilClass) as a first-class benign value; File::NULL; BasicObject + method_missing black hole
implementation_notes: Ruby already implements the pattern for absence: nil is an ordinary object of class NilClass whose methods answer benignly - nil.to_a is [], nil.to_s is '', nil.to_h is {}, nil.to_c and nil.to_r are zero - so callers can often treat a missing value and a present one alike without a special class. For 'discard this output' the standard library ships File::NULL, the platform's null device, which Logger accepts directly (Logger.new(File::NULL) is the idiomatic no-op log); for interfaces that cannot be enumerated, a BasicObject with a method_missing returning self absorbs every call. Write an explicit special-case class only when the degenerate state carries domain meaning, such as an UnknownCustomer with a name and a billing plan.
code_sketch:
class UnknownCustomer
  def name     = "occupant"
  def balance  = BigDecimal(0)
  def bills    = [].freeze
  def unknown? = true
end
UNKNOWN_CUSTOMER = UnknownCustomer.new.freeze

logger = Logger.new(File::NULL)   # stdlib null device: nothing is written
pitfalls: nil is not 'an unknown customer': any method NilClass does not define raises NoMethodError, so the free ride only covers the operations nil itself implements.
A method_missing black hole also absorbs typos and cannot be distinguished from a real implementation by respond_to? unless respond_to_missing? is implemented.
Shared special-case instances must be frozen; Ruby objects are mutable by default, and an accidentally mutated UNKNOWN_CUSTOMER becomes process-global state.
Rails' Object#try and safe navigation (x&.name) remove the need for many special cases at the call site, so check whether the pattern is still buying anything before adding a class.
